1.pericope_label: The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: he shall enter into peace; they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness

schools.summary: Dates the passage to a persecution of the prophets and reads it as a deliverance from worse evils, keeping the shift of number in the text and rendering the last clause of the promise as walking straight before him.
Guards the verb from any suggestion that the righteous can perish eternally, and enumerates the peace that is entered.
Divides between an emendation that recovers a perfect man from the consonants and a plain reading that lets the change of number stand as prophetic idiom.
Turns the removal of good men into a doctrine of providence and reproves the world for not laying it to heart.

debates.question: Who is the righteous man that perishes?

positions.view: the godly generally, taken away before the judgment falls; the perishing is of the outward man only
the righteous survivors of a former reign, the singular pointing to a few conspicuous sufferers who had vexed their souls to death over the evils around them

Christ himself, since an emphasis in the Hebrew points out a particular person and few places in this book do not intend him; the merciful men gathered after him are the apostles, and the evil to come the destruction by Rome

debates.question: Should the change of number in the second verse be emended away?

positions.view: yes: divide one word to recover the perfect man, read the verb as singular on manuscript and version authority, and the supplied words each one may then be spared
no, the sudden change of number is very frequent in the prophets
keep both numbers, and render the last clause as everyone who has walked straight before him, that is, taken the straight path of duty

outliers.reading: Derives the sense of the verb from the straying of cattle passing from one pasture to another and from the Latin for going through, so that the righteous man passes through life and goes before other men into the eternal world, comparing older English idioms in which a man who died went out of sight or fared forth.

Reads the removal as a two-sided providence, in compassion to those taken, who are called into the ark before the deluge, and in wrath to those left, since it is a sign that God intends war when he calls home his ambassadors.

themes: The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come.
He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness.

3.pericope_label: But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress: enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys; among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion

schools.summary: Argues from the details of the scene that the setting is Palestinian and pre-exilic, illustrates the verb of inflaming from the derivation of fanatic, and traces the stone cult to its Phoenician name and to the worship of the powers of nature.
Reads the indictment as an allegory of Rome throughout, and notes a play between the words for smooth stones and for portion that will not come into English.
Documents the worship of anointed stones from ancient writers and from a living parallel, and keeps the sense plain elsewhere, that the descent charged is one of imitation and not of birth.
Makes the sin itself sorcery and adultery, and presses the arraignment with domestic comparisons: a carved way-mark worshipped, children's tables robbed to supply the altars.

debates.question: Where and when does the speaker stand?

positions.view: the prophet looks back from the standpoint of the captivity, addressing the people of the exile about an idolatry handed down from their ancestors, though taking his colours from his own day
the setting is Palestinian: the slaying of children leaves no trace of revival among the exiles or after the return, and the torrent-stream and the clefts of the rock belong distinctively to the land
the generation contemporary with the prophet, summoned to hear its character and its doom

debates.question: Are the sorceress and the adulterer literal or figurative?

positions.view: possibly literal as well as figurative, with reference to the female soothsayers described elsewhere
figurative descent by imitation and not by propagation, their dispositions suiting a bastard brood better than the seed of Abraham
figurative and moral: sin is itself sorcery and adultery, being a departure from God and a dealing with the devil

outliers.reading: Assembles a dossier on the worship of rude consecrated stones, tracing it to the pillar anointed at Bethel that gave the Phoenician baetyls their name, and citing a Church Father confessing that before his conversion he would flatter and petition any smooth stone found smeared with oil, another using the worshipper of every smooth stone as a proverb, a Greek character-sketch of the superstitious man pouring oil in the street and kneeling, and a living parallel in the sacred stones of India.
Illustrates the verb of inflaming from the derivation of fanatic as one heated about a shrine, and says no word better describes the orgiastic excitement of heathen rites.

themes: But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the whore.
Against whom do ye sport yourselves? against whom make ye a wide mouth, and draw out the tongue? are ye not children of transgression, a seed of falsehood,
Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks?
Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion; they, they are thy lot: even to them hast thou poured a drink offering, thou hast offered a meat offering. Should I receive comfort in these?

7.pericope_label: Upon a lofty and high mountain hast thou set thy bed: and thou wentest to the king with ointment, and didst debase thyself even unto hell. When thou criest, let thy companies deliver thee; but he that putteth his trust in me shall possess the land

schools.summary: Weighs each crux in turn, the memorial behind the door, the king visited with ointment, the weariness of the long journey and the ironical righteousness, keeping the received text at every point and glossing the disputed word for hope from Arabic cognates.
Reads the whole indictment as an allegory of Rome, finding the seven hills in the mountain, crucifixes in the household memorials and the last anointing in the ointment carried to the king.

Divides between a textual critic who would reverse the denial of hope and emend two further clauses, and a paraphrast who takes the king for Assyria named by eminency and marks where the charge turns from idolatry to foreign alliance.

Heaps the idol-gods and the confederate troops together as one class of useless helpers and lets the wind have them, since they have made themselves chaff and vanity is both what they are and what shall take them away.

debates.question: What is the remembrance set behind the door and the post?

positions.view: the declaration that the Lord alone is God, the text that belonged on the door-post and has been pushed out of sight
the image of a household god, set privately in defiance of the curse the law pronounces on whoever puts a graven image in a secret place
the memorial text is the common and tenable explanation, but an idolatrous symbol substituted for it is equally possible

debates.question: Who is the king visited with ointment?

positions.view: the king of Assyria, named by eminency, so that the charge turns here from idolatry to confidence in heathen princes

a single letter's change would give Molech, which may even be the sense as the text stands, though the setting makes the Assyrian more natural and the ointment the treasure lavished to buy that alliance
Assyria or Egypt, the ointment being the customary present without which no one in the east approaches a great man
the kings of the earth generally, the singular standing for the plural

debates.question: Should the denial of hope be reversed?

positions.view: yes: a manuscript leaves the negative unpointed as suspect, and two parallel places show a desperate resolve to go on at all hazards, so the true reading is that she said there is hope
no: keep the text but render the noun as result rather than hope, so that Judah would not admit the negotiations were fruitless
keep the text, the word being illuminated by Arabic cognates in which hoping grows out of stretching and drawing out while despairing is literally a drawing in

outliers.reading: Reads the whole passage as an allegory of the church of Rome, finding the seven hills in the lofty mountain, crucifixes and tutelar images in the household memorials, the last anointing in the ointment carried to the king, and the assembled kings in the companies called on to save her.

Proposes a second emendation in the same passage, reading not even of old but and winked, on the authority of twenty-three manuscripts and the ancient versions, and holds that a reading so confirmed admits of no doubt.

themes: Upon a lofty and high mountain hast thou set thy bed: even thither wentest thou up to offer sacrifice.

Behind the doors also and the posts hast thou set up thy remembrance: for thou hast discovered thyself to another than me, and art gone up; thou hast enlarged thy bed, and made thee a covenant with them; thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it.
And thou wentest to the king with ointment, and didst increase thy perfumes, and didst send thy messengers far off, and didst debase thyself even unto hell.
Thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way; yet saidst thou not, There is no hope: thou hast found the life of thine hand; therefore thou wast not grieved.
And of whom hast thou been afraid or feared, that thou hast lied, and hast not remembered me, nor laid it to thy heart? have not I held my peace even of old, and thou fearest me not?
I will declare thy righteousness, and thy works; for they shall not profit thee.

When thou criest, let thy companies deliver thee; but the wind shall carry them all away; vanity shall take them: but he that putteth his trust in me shall possess the land, and shall inherit my holy mountain;

14.pericope_label: Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way: for thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, I dwell with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit. Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near; but there is no peace to the wicked

schools.summary: Settles the disputed half-verse by grammar rather than parallel, leaves the crier of the summons deliberately unnamed, keeps the received text on covetousness, and notices that the manuscripts vary in the closing formula as if copyists had shrunk from the prophet's boldness.

Applies the reproach of covetousness forward to the ministers of the reformed churches, and reads the refusal of peace as excluding the wicked from the church's latter-day prosperity as well as from peace of conscience.
Divides again between an emendation that would make the wrath short-lived rather than caused by covetousness, and a plain reading that lets the doubled word stand for certainty.
Traces covetousness to spiritual idolatry in men who worshipped no images, and closes on the terrors of conscience that make such men a burden to themselves.

debates.question: Who gives the order to clear the road?

positions.view: God himself, the verb to be pointed as a first person future, since the verse closes with my people
a heavenly crier whom the prophet deliberately leaves unidentified, the same appeal recurring once in each of the three books of these prophecies
a voice heard behind the prophet, bringing an oracle from heaven that renews the herald's cry of an earlier chapter
a man whom God will raise up to say it with authority and effect

debates.question: What is the iniquity for which God was wroth?

positions.view: covetousness, literally gain, the root-evil out of which the rest sprang, and a spiritual idolatry that carried away even those who worshipped no images

not covetousness at all: read the word as a little while, following the Greek, so that the sense is that God was wroth for a short time; the Latin rendering that all others follow is quite beside the purpose
the sin is real, and the reproach falls on the ministers of the reformed churches who seek benefices and pluralities and take oversight of the flock for lucre

outliers.reading: Notices that the manuscripts and versions vary at the close between my God, God, and the Lord God, as if transcribers had shrunk from the prophet's boldness in claiming God as in some special sense his own, and suggests that the troubled sea of the image may be the Dead Sea casting up its deposits.

Says the learned have taken great pains to little purpose over the obscure half-verse about the failing spirit, and settles it instead by two passages of the Psalms which he prints as exactly parallel, then distinguishes the animal life from the immortal spirits and notes that one ancient version read a resurrection into the place.

themes: And shall say, Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people.

For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
For I will not contend for ever, neither will I be always wroth: for the spirit should fail before me, and the souls which I have made.
For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth, and smote him: I hid me, and was wroth, and he went on frowardly in the way of his heart.
I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners.
I create the fruit of the lips; Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the Lord; and I will heal him.
But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.
There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.
